evaluation.positioning_hook: A grief-stricken Catholic father hunts the crime family that murdered his wife and children, while his cop sister races to stop him before vengeance consumes the last of their family.

audience_appeal_marketability.reasoning: The revenge-and-grief engine is immediately legible, and the Catholic framing gives it a distinct emotional lane. The audience is clear, but the script is still a hard sell as a very dark, dialogue-heavy crime tragedy rather than a broad commercial thriller.

conceptual_hook_clarity.reasoning: The opening massacre, the time-jump, and Jacob’s escalating hunt make the premise easy to explain in two sentences. The Risaldi family, the sister-cop counterpoint, and the confession/vengeance tension all land early and cleanly.

character_appeal_and_long_term_potential.reasoning: Jacob and Jodie are strong opposing engines: one is grief turned into action, the other is duty turned into desperation. Victor and Ethan add real pressure, though some of the family members function more as archetypal forces than fully surprising people.

creative_originality_and_boldness.reasoning: The script’s Catholic ritual language, confession structure, and choir/music motifs give it a specific identity. It’s bold in emotional scale and moral posture, though the underlying revenge-crime spine is familiar.

narrative_momentum_engagement.reasoning: The story keeps moving through raids, interrogations, confrontations, and escalating family betrayals, with clear forward pressure toward the mansion finale. Some middle passages lean on dialogue and thematic exchange more than plot turns, but the engine stays active.

resonant_originality.reasoning: The combination of Catholic absolution, family annihilation, and organized-crime reckoning feels fresh enough to register quickly. The emotional logic is strong, even if the revenge framework itself is familiar.

world_density_and_texture.reasoning: The world has a real social hierarchy: police, mayor, church, docks, club, mansion, and the Risaldi criminal ecosystem all interlock. The city feels story-generating, though the script is still more focused on the central family war than on a broader civic ecosystem.

tonal_specificity.reasoning: The script has a very specific register: devotional, operatic, brutal, and mournful, with hymns and confession scenes cutting against graphic violence. That tonal blend is hard to mistake for generic crime writing.

latent_depth_slow_burn_potential.reasoning: The faith language, guilt, and family trauma suggest more beneath the surface than a standard revenge piece. The script keeps returning to sin, grace, and identity, which gives it more aftertaste than a simple body-count thriller.

relationship_density_and_ensemble_engine.reasoning: Jacob/Jodie, Jacob/Ethan, Ethan/Victor, and Victor/Alicia all generate distinct dramatic material, and the family structure creates constant cross-pressure. The script is built on relational collisions, not just plot mechanics.

lead_characters.name: Jacob Smith
lead_characters.demographics: Male, late 30s to early 40s, Catholic, working-class father, grieving widower/brother.
lead_characters.hook: Jacob is a devout, emotionally shattered family man whose grief curdles into a private crusade for justice. He reads as gentle and prayerful in the chapel, then terrifyingly single-minded once he decides the law will not be enough; the role lives in that contradiction between tenderness and violence.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Casey Affleck in Manchester by the Sea or Joel Edgerton in The Gift: a contained, wounded man whose silence and restraint carry as much weight as the explosions. It gives an actor the chance to play grief, moral collapse, and physical menace in the same frame.

lead_characters.name: Jodie Smith
lead_characters.demographics: Female, late 30s, police officer, Catholic, Jacob’s sister.
lead_characters.hook: Jodie is a work-obsessed cop who uses the job to outrun grief, then discovers the job is the only thing keeping her from falling apart. She’s tough, defensive, and deeply loyal, but the script keeps exposing how much of her identity is built around being needed and being right.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gave Amy Adams in Sharp Objects or Regina King in If Beale Street Could Talk a chance to play authority, fragility, and emotional containment at once. It’s a strong prestige-supporting turn with real scene ownership opposite the lead.

lead_characters.name: Victor Risaldi
lead_characters.demographics: Male, late 60s, crime patriarch, father, married, commanding.
lead_characters.hook: Victor is the family’s cold center of gravity: elegant, cruel, and convinced that domination is a moral order. He treats his sons like disposable instruments and his wife like property, which makes him less a gangster than a theology of power in human form.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that lets an actor do Brian Cox in Succession or Ben Kingsley in Sexy Beast: authority as performance, menace as intelligence. It’s a delicious villain part with monologue weight and a real final-act payoff.

lead_characters.name: Ethan Risaldi
lead_characters.demographics: Male, late 20s, morally conflicted, Catholic-adjacent, younger brother in the crime family.
lead_characters.hook: Ethan is the family’s conscience, but not in a clean or heroic way; he’s compromised, frightened, and trying to talk himself into being better while still surviving the machine. He becomes the script’s bridge between the church language and the criminal world, which makes him both useful and tragic.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of conflicted, spiritually torn role that gave Paul Dano in Prisoners or Jesse Plemons in The Power of the Dog a lot of interiority to play. It’s a great showcase for an actor who can hold fear, intelligence, and moral shame in the same beat.

lead_characters.name: Martin Risaldi
lead_characters.demographics: Male, early 30s, violent enforcer, son in the crime family.
lead_characters.hook: Martin is the family’s most openly damaged weapon: volatile, sadistic, and desperate to be seen as worthy by a father who only knows how to humiliate. He’s the script’s most immediate embodiment of inherited brutality, and the role turns on how quickly wounded pride becomes cruelty.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of feral, unstable part that gives an actor the same kind of showcase Michael Shannon got in Take Shelter or Jack O’Connell in Starred Up. It’s a high-voltage supporting role with real volatility and scene-stealing potential.

lead_characters.name: Frankie Risaldi
lead_characters.demographics: Male, late 20s to early 30s, crime-family son, more compliant than the others.
lead_characters.hook: Frankie is the family member who still wants to believe obedience can keep him safe, which makes him tragically vulnerable. He’s less monstrous than the others, but the script uses that softness to show how the system eats even the ones who try to cooperate.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that lets an actor do the anxious, cornered work of a Michael C. Hall in Dexter or a Shea Whigham in Boardwalk Empire supporting turn. It’s a pressure-cooker part with a strong collapse trajectory.

lead_characters.name: Edward Risaldi
lead_characters.hook: Edward is the family’s blunt instrument, all muscle and obedience, with just enough interior hesitation to make him unsettling. He’s not the loudest monster in the room, which is exactly why he lands as dangerous: he does what he’s told without needing to believe it.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of physically intimidating role that gives an actor a chance to do the silent menace of Michael Mando in Better Call Saul or Tom Hardy in supporting-mode crime work. The part is lean, brutal, and memorable.

lead_characters.name: Alicia Risaldi
lead_characters.demographics: Female, mid 50s, Victor’s wife, former stripper, mother.
lead_characters.hook: Alicia is trapped inside the family’s hierarchy but still carries the emotional truth of the house, especially around Marcus. She’s one of the script’s most painful figures because she understands the violence and still has to survive it in place.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of bruised, lived-in role that gives an actor the emotional authority of Patricia Clarkson in Sharp Objects or J. Smith-Cameron in Succession. It’s a devastating supporting part with real maternal ache.

lead_characters.name: Father Michael
lead_characters.demographics: Male, late 50s, Catholic priest, compassionate, wise.
lead_characters.hook: Father Michael is the script’s moral counterweight, but not a passive one; he actively interprets suffering for the people around him. He gives the film its spiritual vocabulary and its gentlest authority, which makes him feel like a real anchor rather than a symbolic prop.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that lets an actor do the humane gravitas of Mark Rylance in Bridge of Spies or Brendan Gleeson in Calvary. It’s a quiet, scene-owning part with sermon and confession material.

lead_characters.name: Dr. Owens
lead_characters.hook: Dr. Owens is the first person to name Jacob’s pain as something that needs treatment, not just punishment. She’s a small but important pressure point in the script’s emotional architecture, representing the world of care Jacob keeps rejecting.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of compact, intelligent role that gives an actor the grounded authority of Jennifer Ehle in The King’s Speech or Cherry Jones in prestige drama. It’s brief but functional and emotionally precise.

lead_characters.name: Chief Pitts
lead_characters.demographics: Male, late 50s, police chief, experienced, weary.
lead_characters.hook: Chief Pitts is a tired institutional figure who understands too late how badly the system has failed the Smith family and the city. He’s not a villain, but he’s part of the machinery that keeps arriving after the damage is done.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gives an actor the weary authority of Jeffrey Wright in prestige procedural mode or J.K. Simmons in a grounded drama. It’s a solid institutional-support part with moral weight.

lead_characters.name: Captain Ricks
lead_characters.demographics: Male, late 40s to 50s, police captain, hard-edged.
lead_characters.hook: Ricks is the more aggressive face of the police response, the guy who wants results and is willing to push the room toward them. He helps define the institutional pressure around Jodie without becoming a full antagonist.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gives an actor the clipped, procedural authority of Shea Whigham or David Harbour in a law-enforcement part. It’s a clean, functional supporting role with edge.

lead_characters.name: Mayor Adams
lead_characters.hook: Mayor Adams is the public face of civic failure, polished enough to sound reassuring while standing on top of a catastrophe. He gives the script a political layer and a public-relations hypocrisy that sharpens the city’s rot.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that lets an actor play charm turning to panic, like Michael Shannon in a political-supporting turn or a polished TV mayor with teeth. It’s a nice public-facing antagonist-adjacent part.

lead_characters.name: Marcus Risaldi
lead_characters.hook: Marcus is the child the family mythologizes as innocence, which makes him both precious and dangerous to the story’s emotional logic. He’s a living symbol of what the Risaldi system claims to protect, even as it destroys everything around him.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of child role that can become the emotional center of a final-act rescue or reckoning, similar to the child-presence in Room or The Night Of. It’s a high-stakes, innocence-under-threat part.

crime-family roles need distinct physical types

police station, therapy room, apartment, graveyard

technical.vfx_details: Primarily atmospheric work: smoke, fire, snow, and a few stylized transitions/flashback overlays; no major creature or digital-environment load.
technical.sfx_needs: Gunshots, blood hits, fire damage, practical smoke, and a few violent takedowns.

platform_fit.recommended_lane: premium streaming or prestige theatrical crime drama
platform_fit.series_engine_or_release_model: Feature release model: prestige theatrical or streaming original with awards-leaning crime-drama positioning.

budget.note: Contemporary and mostly grounded, but the script needs multiple night exteriors, a large mansion, a club sequence, docks/warehouse action, fire/smoke work, and a snowbound climax.

casting.note: Jacob, Jodie, Victor, and Ethan all need actors who can carry moral intensity without flattening into types, and Marcus adds a child-performance requirement that matters to the ending.

development.note: The script’s emotional and thematic ambition is clear, but the long confession/monologue passages and the repeated moral debates will be a pacing and balance conversation in development.

comp_set.title: The Place Beyond the Pines
comp_set.why_it_comps: Crime-family fallout, generational damage, and a morally bruised male lead pushing through violence toward consequence.

comp_set.title: Calvary

comp_set.title: A Most Violent Year
comp_set.why_it_comps: Prestige crime texture with pressure-cooker family and institutional stakes, anchored by controlled, adult tension.

audience_target.primary_audience: Adults who respond to prestige crime dramas with emotional weight, moral conflict, and Catholic or faith-inflected storytelling.
audience_target.demographics: 35-64, slightly male-skewing but viable with women who like character-forward prestige thrillers; educated streaming/theatrical audience.

budget_tier.note: Contemporary crime drama with a manageable location count, but the mansion, club, docks, church, night work, and fire/smoke climax keep it above micro.

lane_fit.detail: This sits naturally in the adult crime lane where character pain, moral conflict, and strong performances are the selling points. The Catholic framing and operatic violence make it feel more elevated than a standard revenge thriller.

ip_potential.detail: Standalone feature with a closed emotional and narrative arc; no clear sequel or spinoff vector beyond the finished family reckoning.

strengths.dimension_or_area: Catholic ritual gives the crime story a spine.
strengths.what_it_means: The confession, adoration, rosary, and sermon material give the script a distinctive identity that can separate it from standard revenge fare in the marketplace. That makes it especially attractive to buyers looking for prestige crime with a moral or spiritual angle.
strengths.evidence: The confession booth scenes, Father Michael’s sermons, and the repeated Act of Contrition structure the ending.

strengths.dimension_or_area: Jacob is a strong grief-to-violence lead.
strengths.what_it_means: The role gives an actor a clear emotional engine and a real transformation arc, which is exactly what helps a buyer attach talent. It’s the kind of part that can anchor a director-driven feature and sell on performance.
strengths.evidence: Jacob’s therapy breakdown, his alleyway killing of Tyler, and his final confrontation with Victor all track the same wound.

strengths.dimension_or_area: Jodie and Jacob create a loaded sibling engine.
strengths.what_it_means: The brother-sister conflict gives the film a second emotional axis beyond revenge, which broadens the appeal beyond a single protagonist chase. That relationship can attract actors and buyers who want family drama inside a crime frame.
strengths.evidence: Their funeral conversation, the parking-ramp confrontation, and the final ballroom embrace all carry the same unresolved bond.

strengths.dimension_or_area: Victor is a premium villain role.
strengths.what_it_means: A commanding patriarch with monologues, cruelty, and final-act authority is a real packaging asset because it can attract a name actor and elevate the whole project. Buyers understand instantly what kind of menace he brings.
strengths.evidence: The photo-ripping scene, the ballroom humiliation, and the final “meaning” exchange make him the script’s dominant antagonist.

strengths.what_it_means: The final mansion confrontation, the blood-soaked moral reckoning, and the coda of confession and peace give the film a memorable finish that feels bigger than a routine crime ending. That kind of ending helps word of mouth and makes the project easier to position as prestige.
strengths.evidence: The ballroom showdown, Victor’s death, and the final church/restaurant/graveyard montage.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The world feels like a city under pressure.
strengths.what_it_means: Police, mayor, docks, church, club, and protest all create a civic ecosystem rather than a single-room revenge setup. That gives the film a broader adult audience appeal and a more expensive-feeling world without requiring true tentpole scale.
strengths.evidence: The docks raid, mayor press conferences, church vandalism, and public protest scenes all widen the frame.

whats_special.headline: This is a prestige crime feature with a real emotional hook: a grief-stricken Catholic father, a cop sister, and a monstrous family patriarch collide inside a morally charged revenge story. The script’s strongest commercial asset is that it pairs a performance-forward lead role with a distinctive faith-based identity and a contained enough production footprint to stay in the indie lane.

items.area: The opening massacre is extremely hard-R.
items.detail: The killing of Katherine, Finn, Stacy, and Jay is the script’s defining trauma, but it is also the most buyer-sensitive material on the page. That level of child and family violence narrows the audience and will be a real conversation for theatrical and streamer buyers alike.

items.area: The middle leans on speeches more than turns.
items.detail: Several long exchanges in the chapel, therapy room, and ballroom are carrying theme and character at the same time, which can flatten momentum if a buyer feels the movie is pausing to explain itself. The script is strongest when it is moving through confrontation rather than when it is arguing its philosophy in place.

items.area: Jacob’s moral line is intentionally blurry.
items.detail: He is written as both grieving father and executioner, which is thematically rich but commercially tricky because the audience has to stay with a protagonist who repeatedly crosses into murder. That makes the film more prestige-tragic than broadly empathetic, and it will shape who says yes.

items.area: The music clearance list is long.
items.detail: Come Back, Let All Mortal Flesh Keep Silent, O Holy Night, Clair de Lune, 500 Miles, L’amour Toujours, and Good Looking are all named or plot-adjacent, which means the soundtrack budget and clearance plan need to be real, not aspirational. The music is doing emotional work on the page, so it can’t simply be swapped out without affecting the film’s identity.

issues.headline: The script’s biggest friction is that its most memorable set piece is also its most punishing: the opening family slaughter is a severe content gate, not just a dramatic one. Beyond that, the film lives in a prestige lane where the long monologues, heavy moral argument, and music-clearance load will all be part of the greenlight conversation.
